author: Jim Lowe Staff Writer
title: George Frederic Handel's 'Messiah': Tavener's "God is With Us' to add to the drama | Rutland Reader | rutlandherald.com
text:
Alastair Stout is always looking to the dramatic. Minister of music at Rutland’s Grace Congregational Church since 2017, he is introducing this year’s “Messiah” performances with John Tavener’s “God is With Us: A Christmas Proclamation” — at only 5 minutes it packs a wallop!
“What’s wonderful about that is that the Tavener finishes with a huge G major organ chord, and we’re going to segue right into the Symphony of the ‘Messiah’ without any pause,” Stout said. “There will be no moment to take a breath or anything. We’re just going from the glory of the Tavener into this kind of abyss of the opening of the ‘Messiah’.”
But that might not be enough for Stout.
“I’m not sure if I’m going to make it happen or not — add a little bit of tympani to the very first couple of strokes of the Symphony, maybe even a trumpet,” Stout said. “Or just to give that emphasis because the Tavener ends with the most enormous organ chord — every stop the organ has is playing, and it’s this glorious sunrise moment where Christ is born.
“And then from that to just the strings and the woodwinds that play the Symphony, I’m wondering whether that might not be enough,” he said. “We do hire tympani and trumpets, so why not make a little bit more use of them than just having them play a couple of movements?
“But who knows? We’ll see what happens,” Stout said. “That might just be pushing it over the edge — and I might be carted away to jail. Who knows?”
Grace Congregational Church will present the Rutland Area Chorus, orchestra and soloists, in George Frederic Handel’s “Messiah” (Part 1 and “Hallelujah” Chorus), preceded by Tavener’s “God is With Us: A Christmas Proclamation,” at 3:30 and 7 p.m. Sunday, Dec. 14, in the church sanctuary in Rutland.
Vocal soloists are soprano Helen Lyons, mezzo-soprano Amy Frostman, tenor Ryan Mangan and baritone David Rugger.
Handel (1685-1759) wrote “Messiah,” his beloved English-language oratorio, in 1741. The text was compiled from the King James Bible and the Coverdale Psalter by Charles Jennens. First performed in 1742, receiving its London premiere a year later, it has become one of the few musical works performed universally throughout the world.
Jennens’ text, an extended reflection on Jesus as Messiah, begins in Part I with prophecies by Isaiah and others, and moves to the annunciation to the shepherds, the only “scene” taken from the Gospels. Part II concentrates on the Passion of Jesus and ends with the “Hallelujah” chorus. And Part III covers the resurrection of the dead and Christ’s glorification in heaven.
The Rutland Area Chorus will perform the entire Part I, with arias and choral numbers that contemplate the idea of a Messiah, foretell the coming, and hail the arrival. The concert concludes with the beloved “Hallelujah” chorus from Part II.
Sir John Tavener (1944-2013) was a 20th-century English composer best known for his extensive output of sacred choral works including the “Song for Athene,” which was performed at the funeral of Princess Diana in 1997. “God Is With Us” is written for SATB choir, tenor soloist and organ.
The basses open the piece singing a low chant-like passage on the opening line “God is with us.”
“The rest of the choir join and then the solo voice, our wonderful Ryan Mangan, emerges with a bold and highly decorated solo reminiscent of a Middle Eastern style chant,” Stout said. “As the piece progresses, Ryan becomes more artistically free on his line with phrases such as ‘Prince of Peace’ being highly decorated. The choir contribute with variations on the opening refrain, again, becoming more complex before coming together for the last two lines of the text.
“The work ends with a completely unexpected twist — magnificent, Earth shattering and glorious!”
Tavener’s ‘God Is With Us’ was commissioned by Martin Neary, organist at Westminster Abbey.
“This is a piece that I’ve known since I was a little boy, when I was a chorister, and it stayed with me over the years,” Stout said. “It’s not too difficult, but it’s incredibly moving and works really well as a choral piece. It’s eight-part a cappella, which I thought would be a wonderful challenge for the Rutland Area Chorus that haven’t done too much a cappella work. And, of course, that’s how you build a choir and make it better and better, by having them sing more a cappella music, and we do that.”
In fact, the 85-voice Rutland Area Choir has experienced real musical growth this year.
“I think we’ve actually turned the corner in terms of their understanding of how I want (‘Messiah’) shaped,” Stout said. “They’re starting to phrase things much more musically, things like tapering of text, tapering of phrases, shaping the dynamics, I think, in a remarkable way this year more than it has in past years. And I don’t quite know why.”
An extra week of rehearsal helped, as the VSO Holiday Pops coming to Rutland this weekend moved the Grace “Messiah” performance a week later.
“I’ve really enjoyed having a slightly more relaxed rehearsal atmosphere where we can talk a little bit more about the structure of the piece, and Handel’s techniques, and things like that,” Stout said. “I think that really does help the choir understand where I’m coming from.”
Stout held a kind of workshop at a recent rehearsal on the key relationships of each movement, to understand why Handel wrote in those specific keys and how those keys relate to each other.
“And what’s wonderful about that is that the Tavener finishes with a huge G major chord,” he said. “We’re going straight from that enormous organ G major chord right into the relative minor, that E minor, the chaos movement of the Symphony where all hope is lost — before we build up to the arrival of the Messiah.”
